items.excerpt: Here's a rundown of all the news you need to know for Saturday, including US President Donald Trump threatening military action against Iran for a rumored "dirty bomb" plot targeting Washington and downplaying a wave of US outages, Denmark expelling the Russian defense attache and halting non-essential visas for Russian citizens, and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz calling for a "360-degree partnership" with Qatar. US President Donald Trump threatened military action against Iran for a rumored "dirty bomb" plot targeting Washington, saying: "If they do (that), we’re going to fight." He insisted his administration is closely monitoring Tehran and had extensive intelligence on its activities. "We will not allow that." Speaking at his first news conference since returning from Asia, Trump also downplayed a wave of banking, technology, and service outages across the country, attributing many to companies upgrading their systems and saying "they’re all separate events." He blamed air traffic control disruptions on infrastructure that is "55 years old and older" and said his administration is seeking $50 billion from Congress to build a new system. ... - Denmark expels Russian defense attache, halts non-essential visas for Russians Denmark has ordered the Russian defense attache to leave within seven days and will halt all non-essential visas for Russian citizens, according to Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen. He called the expulsion a strong signal to Moscow, adding "enough is enough," and said Denmark is continuing to support Ukraine. Rasmussen said the government plans to lift the obligation to receive ships linked to Russia and would discuss visa restrictions with other Schengen countries, singling out France, while Denmark will not expel all Russian diplomats as it needs to maintain communication with Moscow. ... - Germany's Merz hails strategic ties with Qatar, seeks '360-degree partnership' German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called for a "360-degree partnership" with Qatar, welcoming its pledge to invest an additional €15 billion ($16.5 billion) in Germany and praising its efforts to end the war between the US and Iran. items.title: Fed officials consider faster rate hikes | Features | messenger-inquirer.com
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON (AP) — More evidence this week of hot inflation in the U.S. was unpleasant news for the Federal Reserve, not to mention consumers: Rising prices may be spreading beyond the one-time shocks from tariffs and high gas prices into the wider economy, meaning that mortgages, credit cards and other forms of borrowing are likely to become increasingly expensive. Tuesday's consumer price index report showed broadly rising costs across a range of goods and services, some with little connection to more expensive oil and gas or surging investment in artificial intelligence data centers, another factor blamed for worsening inflation. And there is increasing anxiety among Fed officials that higher oil prices stemming from the Iran war may last longer than previously thought.

items.title: Fed's Cook says rate hikes needed to lower high inflation - The Korea Times
items.excerpt: Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook on Friday made a case for more interest rate hikes, saying the U.S. central bank's current policy rate is not high enough to deal with inflation levels she views with "great concern." "In a different environment, the (Federal Open Market) Committee could afford to be patient, but I continue to believe that in this economic climate we do not have that luxury," given how high inflation is and for how long it has been above the Fed's 2 percent target, Cook said in the text of a speech to be presented at a central bank conference in Chile. Cook said the quarter-percentage-point rate hike the Fed delivered at its September 15-16 policy meeting was not enough to moderate current levels of inflation. What's more, "inflation data received since the September rate increase, including reports last week, fail to provide me with sufficient evidence that inflation is returning to a sustainable path," she said. "There is little evidence inflation is declining." Cook, who voted for a rate hike at that meeting, was one of two Fed officials who dissented over the Fed's decision last month to leave its policy rate in the 3.75 percent-4.00 percent range. Officials at the October 27-28 meeting signaled that inflation remained too high then even as they refrained from action. Regarding her dissent in October, Cook said, "My vote reflected the urgency I feel to tackle inflation," which "has been above target for more than five and a half years, and every additional day poses greater risk that price- and wage-setters will adjust their inflation expectations upward." ... Cook on Friday said the risk of not acting fast enough to lower inflation could bring more pain later. "Waiting longer to implement rate increases risks getting behind the curve," she said. "If we fall behind, additional and larger rate increases may be required later to catch up, which could increase stress on our financial system and have unnecessarily damaging effects on American households." The Fed governor noted that financial conditions remain accommodative and are not providing the needed level of restraint on the economy. Cook, however, was upbeat on the economy. She said growth is "strong and accelerating" and that the job market remains "solid."

items.title: Trump orders federal contractors to notify White House before giving Congress information
items.excerpt: President Donald Trump on Friday ordered companies with federal contracts to alert the White House before sharing information with Congress and to withhold material the administration deems confidential, expanding his efforts to limit congressional oversight ahead of Democrats taking control of Congress in January. Trump's executive order, issued late on Friday, applies to federal contractors and their subcontractors. Companies that fail to comply could face cancellation of existing contracts or suspension from future federal business, it said. The order is part of a broader effort by the Republican president to control what information reaches Congress and limit Democratic investigations into his administration, setting up a potentially significant battle over presidential power and lawmakers' authority to scrutinize the White House. Democrats, who won control of both chambers of Congress in this month's midterm elections, have vowed to investigate Trump's administration, his family's business dealings and its relationships with private companies. Friday's order follows a directive issued this week by White House Counsel Will Scharf requiring federal agencies to obtain White House approval before employees agree to testify before Congress. Scharf said certain Democratic investigations could amount to criminal conduct, a claim that has raised questions about the administration's attempts to limit congressional oversight. The restrictions could face legal challenges, particularly if contractors are told to withhold information sought through congressional subpoenas. Executive privilege allows presidents to protect certain confidential communications, but courts can intervene in disputes over Congress' authority to obtain information. Democrats are preparing to investigate potential conflicts of interest, federal contracts, immigration enforcement and the administration's handling of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation. Representative Robert Garcia of California, who is set to lead the House Oversight Committee, this week asked 12 of Trump's top allies, former aides and family members to preserve documents related to alleged Trump family corruption and government misconduct. ... The White House defended Friday's order as necessary to protect sensitive government communications, including those involving national security. It said contractors responding independently to congressional requests could expose privileged information and force the administration into costly legal disputes.

items.title: Democrats won big in the midterms. So now what? By Reuters
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON, Nov 21 (Reuters) - Democrats basking in their November 3 election wins will soon unveil an ambitious legislative agenda for the first 100 days and beyond, in a test of progressives’ influence and Republicans’ willingness to cooperate, as they take control of the US Congress on January 3. That agenda is likely to be unveiled in early December once a Senate leadership race is settled. It will mark a thunderous reversal of the past two years, when President Donald Trump’s Republicans ruled the Senate and House of Representatives. With their narrow majorities, they rammed through major tax cuts skewed toward the rich and stood by as Trump grabbed their powers over tariffs and spending. Democrats’ new majorities in Congress are anything but narrow. With a 56-44 majority in the Senate they are four votes short of the 60 votes needed to advance most legislation. In the House, their 257-172 force could grow beyond an 85-vote margin once a handful of races are settled. "This is a realignment," said Democratic Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia in a post-election interview with reporters. But in a warning to Democrats, veteran Republican Senator John Boozman of Arkansas said in an interview that despite his party’s losses across the United States, Trump remains "a powerful force" and "I don’t see any of his vetoes getting overridden" by Congress during his remaining two years in office. ... For months, Democrats have been plotting a House-Senate coordinated attack to undo Trump’s major accomplishments, according to lawmakers and aides. With the high cost of living the top concern voiced by voters, Democratic leaders are going after the low-hanging fruit that also would help unite their party’s progressives and moderates. Early votes are expected on legislation handcuffing Trump’s ability to wage war on Iran without Congress’ approval, which would help lower gasoline prices. Reversing Republicans’ deep cuts to Medicaid and SNAP food stamp programs would begin helping the poor meet healthcare and grocery costs. Meanwhile, progressives have urged raising the federal minimum wage, which is unchanged since 2009 at $7.25 per hour. Some are pushing for $20 to $25. And in response to voter disgust over Washington ethics breaches, one of the first bills Democrats are expected to present is one barring lawmakers from insider trading of stocks. Republicans face a bind: joining Democrats could anger Trump unless he backs measures, while stonewalling could anger voters.

Michael Showalter directs. The film updates the setting to the present day rather than rebooting the story. Variety reported the casting on 20 November, and no release date has been announced. Ahan Shetty has joined Vikram Bhatt’s 1920: Cold Winter, the sixth film in the 1920 horror franchise. Filming runs from December 2026 to March 2027 in Ooty and Mumbai. Pooja Sharma and Ashok Darji are to star in Nepali film Seto Coat, officially announced on 20 November. Filming begins on 25 November 2026. Advance booking opened for Paral Ko Aago ahead of its nationwide release on Friday 20 November, with over 100 shows secured. Suhana Thapa, Saugat Malla and Prakash Saput star in the film, inspired by a story by Guru Prasad Mainali. ## Box office Drishyam 3 has closed its theatrical run with Rs 594.89 crore worldwide and Rs 381.32 crore net in India, on a reported Rs 110 crore budget, a return of 246.65 percent. Koimoi ranks it the highest-grossing threequel. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping took an estimated $51 million on Friday, including $21 million from Thursday previews. Deadline projects a $110 million domestic opening weekend. Final numbers are due on Monday. ## Deaths E.J. Carroll, the veteran character and voice actor known for The Deuce, Law & Order and Boardwalk Empire, has died aged 66. He died suddenly on Thursday 19 November on his way to a voiceover recording session. His manager confirmed the death to TheWrap, and no cause of death has been determined.

items.title: Egyptian Music Star Mohamed Mounir Gets Biopic – Doha Industry Days
items.excerpt: The life and legacy of legendary Egyptian artist Mohamed Mounir is set to be explored in a biopic spearheaded by The Film Committee at Media City Qatar. The Film Committee has acquired the rights to document Mounir’s life story, with partners on the project set to include a leading regional studio and other partners, which have yet to be unveiled. The project was announced at the Film Committee’s Doha Industry Days, just hours after the Qatari body gave an update on previously announced biopic Caesar, about Syrian whistleblower Farid Al-Madhhan, announcing Taim Hasan as it star. Mounir’s career spans nearly five decades across music, film and television. ... The Film Committee said the biopic will trace Mounir’s journey from his humble beginnings to becoming one of the Arab world’s most celebrated and influential artists, revealing untold details, surprises, stories and anecdotes. ... With development in the early stages, the hunt is now on for an actor to play Mounir.
